_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. status: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship, cite in note), 'provisional' (my romanization, not found outside; builder marks it), 'decided' (a project style call). Sections are rendered as glossary headings; keys starting with '_' are ignored.

郁慕俠.cast: The author: a Shanghai newspaperman of the 1920s-30s, whose beat was the treaty-port city's low life and slang.
郁慕俠.note: Pen name of the journalist and tabloid (xiaobao) writer who compiled these sketches; the surname is Yu (郁). Active in the Shanghai small-paper press of the 1920s and 1930s.

天虛我生.note: The pen name of Chen Diexian (陳蝶仙, 1879–1940), a prolific novelist of the “Mandarin Ducks and Butterflies” school, editor of the Shenbao’s literary supplement, and industrialist who founded Household Industries (家庭工業社), maker of Butterfly-brand toothpowder. He wrote this preface.

袁世凱.note: The strongman of the early Republic (1859-1916): last great minister of the Qing, first President of the Republic, and, in 1915-16, would-be emperor under the reign-title Hongxian.

戴季陶.note: Journalist turned Nationalist ideologue (1891-1949); in these years a firebrand writer under the pen name Tianchou, later a founding theorist of the Kuomintang and long-serving President of the Examination Yuan.

周浩.note: Journalist, styled Shaoheng; co-founder and director (with Dai Jitao) of the Shanghai Minquan Bao in 1912.

趙秉鈞.note: Yuan Shikai's premier and interior minister, implicated in the 1913 assassination of Song Jiaoren; died suddenly in 1914.

康有為.note: Leader of the 1898 Hundred Days Reform and thereafter a lifelong constitutional monarchist (1858-1927).

梁啟超/啟超/梁任公.note: Kang Youwei's foremost disciple (1873-1929), reformer, journalist and scholar; unlike his teacher he served in Republican cabinets.

章太炎.note: Zhang Binglin (1869-1936), the great philologist and revolutionary polemicist, jailed in the 1903 Subao case.

鄭正秋.note: Pioneer of modern Chinese theater and film (1889-1935); organizer of the Xinmin drama society and, later, a founder of the Mingxing Film Company.

歐陽予倩.note: Actor, playwright and dramatist (1889-1962), one of the founders of modern Chinese spoken drama.

蘇石癡.note: New-drama impresario of the 1910s; head of the Minxing society.

辜鴻銘.note: 1857-1928, the Penang-born, Western-educated scholar and eccentric who became the most famous conservative apologist for Confucian China; notorious in his own day for defending foot-binding and concubinage.

薛大塊頭.note: A nickname (literally 'Xue the big lump'); a noted Shanghai procurer of an earlier day, as the author presents him.

寄生姆媽.note: A demimonde nickname for a procuress: 'parasite' plus the Wu word for mother/madam.

聞鶯.note: A woman physiognomist whose murder was a Shanghai sensation of the early 1930s, as the author reports it.

菱清.note: A woman physiognomist, partner of Wenying on the surviving flyer the author describes.

張桐花.note: Styled Yiming; engaged as director of the 1920 courtesan poll, as the author reports.

吳書箴.note: Proprietor of the Shanghai tabloid Dianguang Ribao, as the author reports.

譚鑫培.note: The reigning Peking-opera laosheng (bearded-male-role) master (1847–1917); stage name Xiao Jiaotian.

小叫天.note: Stage name of Tan Xinpei; literally 'Little Cry-to-Heaven.'

黃楚九.note: Shanghai patent-medicine magnate and amusement-hall impresario (1872–1931).

賽金花.note: Celebrated late-Qing courtesan, legendary figure of the Boxer year.

夏月潤.note: Peking-opera actor, co-founder with his brother of Shanghai's reformist New Stage.

夏月珊.note: Peking-opera actor, co-founder of the New Stage; brother of Xia Yuerun.

林黛玉.note: The late-Qing Shanghai courtesan who took this stage name (not the heroine of Dream of the Red Chamber).

經營三.note: The merchant who financed and built the New World with Huang Chujiu and ran it alone after Huang left. The reprint misprints his name 經潤三 as 經營三.

陸遜.note: The general of Wu (183–245), NOT the modern writer Lu Xun 魯迅 (different characters, different tone).

周瑜.note: The young admiral of Wu (175–210) who broke Cao Cao's fleet at the Red Cliffs.

立德.note: R. W. Little, founder of the Shanghai Electric Company (1882), China's first power plant.

皮曉浦.note: The Westerner the author credits with the first Shanghai telephone exchange (1882); identity unverified.

能慕谷.note: A French Jesuit father of the Zikawei (Xujiahui) Observatory; transliteration of his name.

黃式權.note: Late-Qing Shanghai journalist, author of sketches of the city.

孔夫子.note: Confucius (551–479 BC); here the name of a Yangtze steamer.

左宗棠.note: Great Qing statesman-general (1812–1885), later Governor-General of the Two Jiang.

南京路.note: The premier commercial street of the International Settlement; older English “Nanking Road.”

南市.note: The old walled Chinese city of Shanghai and the district around it, south of the foreign concessions.

城隍廟.note: The temple of the city's tutelary god (chenghuang) in the old Chinese city; the Shanghai City God Temple and the bazaar around it were a great popular resort.

虹廟.note: A popular temple on (East) Nanjing Road, properly the Bao’an Situ Temple (保安司徒廟), enshrining Guanyin; famous for its dense incense-smoke, and much frequented by Shanghai courtesans.

西湖.note: The famous scenic lake at Hangzhou.

金陵.note: Jinling, a classical name for Nanjing, capital of the Nationalist government from 1927.

福州路.note: The Shanghai street popularly called Fourth Avenue (Simalu), lined with bookshops, teahouses and brothels.

望平街.note: The short Shanghai lane, off Nanjing Road, that housed the great newspaper offices; known as Newspaper Street.

棋盤街.note: A street near Nanjing Road, famous for its bookshops and publishers.

四馬路.note: The old popular name of Fuzhou Road (see the glossary entry 福州路), the International Settlement's street of publishers, theatres and courtesan houses.

靜安寺路.note: The road running west from the racecourse to the Bubbling Well (Jing'an Temple); now Nanjing West Road.

北四川路.note: A street running north out of the International Settlement into the Hongkou district, with a large Japanese population and, as the author says, many hidden vice-dens.

霞飛路.note: The main avenue of the French Concession, centre of the White Russian emigre quarter; now Huaihai Road.

靶子路.note: A Hongkou street named for the old rifle range; now Wujin Road.

漕涇.note: A market town southwest of the city (now in Jinshan district), a country retreat well outside the settlements.

三馬路.note: Hankou Road, third of the numbered 'Avenues' running back from the Bund; see the note on the avenue-numbering at 'Third Avenue'.

張園.note: The famous public pleasure-garden of late-Qing and early-Republican Shanghai; also called the Weiyuan.

味蒓園.note: Literary alternate name of Zhang's Garden.

愚園.note: A private pleasure-garden on Edinburgh Road (not the old City-God-Temple Yu Garden of Nanshi).

半淞園.note: A riverside pleasure-garden in Nanshi, opened 1918.

安塏第.note: The tall landmark building of Zhang's Garden; its English name was Arcadia Hall.

寶昌路.note: The pre-1915 name of Avenue Joffre.

九畝地.note: A district of old Shanghai's Zhabei theater quarter; literally 'Nine-Mu Land.'

法國公園.note: The French Concession's public park (Koukaza Park), now Fuxing Park (復興公園).

泥城橋.note: The bridge over the old Defense Creek at the north-western corner of the International Settlement, by the Racecourse; the creek was later filled in and the name survives as a district.

跑馬廳.note: The Shanghai Race Club's course, the great turf oval at the heart of the Settlement (today People's Square and People's Park).

外白渡橋.note: The steel-truss bridge (1907) at the mouth of Suzhou Creek, north end of the Bund; the foreigners' Garden Bridge.

蘇州河.note: The lower course of the Wusong River as it runs through Shanghai to meet the Huangpu at the Bund.

馬霍路.note: A cross-street off Bubbling Well Road in the western Settlement; today North Huangpi Road.

顧家宅.note: The French-Concession district where the French Park lies; 'Koukaza' in French usage.

兆豐公園.note: The largest Settlement park (opened 1914), at the west end of Bubbling Well Road; today Zhongshan Park.

十六浦.note: The 'Sixteenth Wharf' district on the Huangpu waterfront, east of the old walled city.

徐家匯.note: The Jesuit centre (Zikawei) in south-west Shanghai: cathedral, college and observatory.

松江.note: The old prefectural city south-west of Shanghai, and its examination seat.

愛多亞路.note: The boundary street between the Settlement and the French Concession; today East Yan'an Road.

寧紹.note: The prefectures of Ningbo and Shaoxing in eastern Zhejiang.

租界.note: The foreign-administered concession areas of Shanghai — chiefly the International Settlement and the French Concession — each with its own council, police, and by-laws.

捕房.note: A police station of the concession forces (the Settlement’s Municipal Police, or the French Concession police).

探捕.note: A plain-clothes detective or constable of the concession police.

錢莊.note: A traditional Chinese money-shop or bank (qianzhuang), as distinct from the foreign banks; the mainstay of Chinese commercial credit.

民立報.note: The leading revolutionary daily of the late Qing, founded in Shanghai by Yu Youren in 1910.

民權報.note: A fiercely anti-Yuan Shanghai daily of 1912-13, run by Zhou Hao with Dai Jitao as chief writer.

天鐸報.note: A Shanghai daily of the late Qing and early Republic that turned to revolutionary commentary; an early berth for Dai Jitao, Zhou Hao and Chen Bulei.

亞細亞報.note: The Shanghai Yaxiya Ribao (Asia Daily), a pro-Yuan paper that promoted his monarchy in 1915-16.

大晚報.note: An independent Shanghai evening paper founded by Zhang Zhuping in 1932.

申報.note: Shanghai's oldest and most important Chinese daily (founded 1872).

新聞報.note: A major Shanghai commercial daily, rival of the Shenbao.

永安公司.note: Wing On, the great Cantonese-owned department store on Nanjing Road (opened 1918), whose roof-garden amusement hall was the Tianyun Tower.

電光日報.note: The 'Electric Light Daily', a small Shanghai tabloid, as the author reports; no independent record traced.

先施公司.note: The earliest of the great Nanjing Road department stores (opened 1917), with a rooftop amusement hall.

新新公司.note: One of the four great Nanjing Road department stores (opened 1926), with a rooftop garden.

新舞臺.note: The pioneering reformed theater at Jiumudi, founded 1908 by the Xia brothers.

新世界.note: A large amusement hall at the corner of Bubbling Well Road, opened 1915.

群仙.note: An all-girl opera house on Fourth Avenue.

樓外樓.note: Huang Chujiu's rooftop amusement garden of 1912, atop the New-New Stage on Nanjing Road; the first of its kind in Shanghai.

大世界.note: The amusement palace Huang Chujiu opened in 1917 after leaving the New World; long the most famous in Shanghai.

工部局.note: The Shanghai Municipal Council, governing body of the International Settlement (1854–1943); its Chinese name means 'Board of Works'.

公董局.note: The governing council of the French Concession, counterpart to the Settlement's Municipal Council.

水爐公所.note: The trade guild of the boiled-water shops.

冠雲詩社.note: A poem-riddle house on Avenue Édouard VII, the last of its kind at the time of writing.

大廠.note: The gamblers' name for the huahui bank (also datong, 'the big tube').

國曆.note: The Gregorian (solar) calendar, adopted by the Republic on 1 January 1912 as the guoli, “national calendar.”

陰曆.note: The traditional lunisolar calendar (also called the old calendar, jiuli), which set the dates of the traditional New Year and festivals.

財神.note: The god of wealth, welcomed into shops and homes at the New Year to secure a prosperous year of trade.

接路頭.note: The Shanghai term for welcoming the God of Wealth; lutou (“road-head”) is the local name of the god. Kept on the night of the fourth day of the first month.

元宵.note: The fifteenth of the first lunar month, the last day of the New Year season.

元旦.note: Here the first day of the first lunar month — the traditional New Year — not the Gregorian 1 January.

菩薩.note: In popular speech any temple god or idol, not only a Buddhist bodhisattva.

小洋.note: Subsidiary silver coin (dimes and twenty-cent pieces), which passed at a slight discount to the standard silver dollar (dayang).

元寶茶.note: New Year tea served with two olives on the lid, the olives standing for silver ingots (yuanbao) — an auspicious wish for wealth.

壓歲錢.note: New Year money given by elders to children, “to weigh down the year” (and, by a pun on sui, to ward off evil); the Shanghai word in the text is yasui dian (壓歲鈿), dian being the Wu-dialect word for money.

新劇.note: Early modern Chinese spoken drama (huaju), as against sung opera; in its first years popularly the 'civilized play' (wenmingxi).

遊戲場.note: A Shanghai indoor amusement arcade (like the Great World), offering variety turns, opera, films and games under one roof.

小報.note: The small-format Shanghai 'mosquito papers' of gossip, entertainment and scandal.

號外.note: A special one-sheet newspaper edition rushed out to carry breaking news.

野雞.note: Literally 'wild chicken', the Shanghai term for the lowest, unlicensed street prostitute; see the fuller note at ch012. Their houses were the third grade (see the note on the house-grades).

么二.note: The second grade of courtesan house ('one-two'); see the note on the house-grades at ch019.

長三.note: The first, highest grade of courtesan house ('long three'); see the note on the house-grades at ch019.

堂子.note: A courtesan house or brothel; the ordinary Shanghai word.

鹹肉莊.note: Literally 'salted-meat house', slang for a cheap brothel; 'salt-meat' (a preserved, second-rate cut) is demimonde slang for a prostitute.

鹹肉.note: 'Salted meat', demimonde slang for a prostitute; hence 'Russian salt-meat', 'Korean salt-meat' for foreign prostitutes.

花煙間.note: The lowest grade of brothel, where opium ('smoke') and sex were sold together; see the chapter of that name (ch033).

煙妓.note: A prostitute of a flower-smoke room, who served opium.

淌白.note: A clandestine, unlicensed prostitute who solicited in the open; a Shanghai term.

姨太太.note: A secondary wife; also called a 'little wife' (小老婆).

小先生.note: A young apprentice courtesan, not yet deflowered; 'master' (先生) was the honorific for a courtesan of the better houses.

舞女.note: A paid dance-hall partner; the rendering settled at ch014.

大洋.note: The standard silver dollar (yuan); 大洋鈿 is 'silver-dollar money'. See the money note at ch001.

白相人.note: Literally 'a man about town / a player'; Shanghai slang for a petty gangster, tout or idler of the streets.

包客.note: A man who 'books' a prostitute for his exclusive use, paying her keep; see the chapter of that name (ch032).

三寸金蓮.note: The elegant name for a woman's bound feet, ideally three Chinese inches long.

髦兒戲.note: Peking-style opera performed entirely by female troupes, all roles included.

鬚生.note: The laosheng, the dignified older-man role type of Peking opera, marked by a beard.

拆字.note: Fortune-telling by dissecting a written Chinese character into its parts.

白俄.note: Anti-Bolshevik Russian émigrés who fled to Shanghai after 1917.

野雞大學.note: A degree-mill; 'pheasant' (yeji) is the Shanghai slang for anything unlicensed and irregular.

八卦.note: The eight three-line figures of the Book of Changes, used in an eight-sided mirror-plaque as an apotropaic charm.

風水.note: Chinese geomancy: the siting of buildings and graves in harmony with the currents of the land.

翁仲.note: The paired stone human statues set along the spirit-way before a grand tomb.

自來火.note: Old Shanghai term for coal gas and gaslight; later also a friction match.

地火.note: The popular nickname for piped coal gas, the 'fire that comes from underground'.

小押當.note: The humblest tier of pawnshop: high interest, short terms, small loans.

餉押.note: A pawnshop originally for soldiers pledging goods against unpaid army wages (餉銀).

老虎灶.note: A neighbourhood shop selling boiled water; a fixture of Shanghai lane life.

弄堂.note: The Shanghai residential lane, and the block of row-houses opening off it.

詩謎.note: A gambling game: bet which character fills a blanked line of classical verse.

大洋盤.note: Shanghai slang for a prize dupe, with a pun on the silver dollar (yang).

花會.note: An illegal numbers-lottery of the Jiangnan region; bet which of some thirty-odd named characters the bank will draw.

快馬.note: The bicycle-runners hired to race the huahui results out to the betting public.

後門貨.note: Stolen property pilfered by warehouse- and shop-hands and slipped out the back to be fenced.

丟圈.note: The fairground hoop-la: pitch a wooden ring over pegged prizes to win them.

丟票.note: A pawnshop swindle: a ticket for worthless pledged goods is dropped in the street to lure a finder into redeeming it.

裱畫店.note: A shop that mounts and frames paintings and calligraphy on scrolls.

換天頭.note: An art-forgery trick using the top margin of a scroll; here, layer-splitting a painting into two.
